source_refs.note: Topic 15.6 (PDF 53-54); Figs 15.11 and 15.13 are redrawn and Fig 15.12 (photograph) is described. The note that the shift occurs at a higher-index surface is added. The check question is Short Answer 15.3, answered; answer needs review.

blocks.text: Bright bands of colour are often seen when light reflects from a thin layer of oil floating on water or from a soap bubble. These are the result of interference. Light waves are reflected from the front and back surfaces of such thin films, and constructive interference between the two reflected waves (which have different path lengths) occurs at different places for different wavelengths. In Fig 15.11, light falling on a thin film of thickness t is partly reflected at the upper surface (path abc); light transmitted through the upper surface is partly reflected at the lower surface (path abdef). The two reflected waves meet at the eye, where, depending on their phase relationship, they may interfere constructively or destructively. Different colours have different wavelengths, so the interference may be constructive for some colours and destructive for others.

That is why we see coloured patterns in thin films, such as the thin soap films that make up bubble walls (the book's Fig 15.12 is a photograph of this) and thin films of oil on water. The complex shapes of the coloured patterns come from variations in the thickness of the film.

Consider monochromatic light reflected from two nearly parallel surfaces at nearly normal incidence. Fig 15.13 shows two glass plates separated by a thin wedge of air. The path difference between the waves reflected from the two surfaces next to the air wedge is twice the thickness t of the wedge at each point. Where 2t is a whole number of wavelengths we expect constructive interference and a bright area; where it is a half-integer number of wavelengths, destructive interference and a dark area. Where the plates touch there is practically no path difference, so we would expect a bright area.

When the experiment is done, bright and dark fringes appear but they are interchanged: along the line where the plates touch there is a dark fringe, not a bright one. This shows that one of the reflected waves undergoes a half-cycle phase shift on reflection, so the two waves reflected at the line of contact are half a cycle out of phase even though their paths are equal. This phase shift can be predicted from Maxwell's equations and the electromagnetic nature of light; it happens when light reflects from a medium of higher refractive index (here, the glass below the air film).

blocks.alt: Top left: a ray in air hits a thin film of thickness t and index n; one ray reflects at the top surface and another, after passing into the film, reflects at the bottom; both travel up towards the eye. Top right: an air wedge between two glass plates, separated at one end by a thin spacer of height h, with alternating dark and red fringe marks above. Bottom: Newton's rings: a plano-convex lens resting on a flat glass plate, and concentric dark and light rings with a dark centre.
blocks.caption: Thin films, the air wedge and Newton's rings (original diagram after Figs 15.11 to 15.15).
blocks.long_description: In each case two reflections, from the top and bottom of a thin layer, interfere. The thickness of the layer sets the path difference; where it is nearly zero, the half-cycle shift on one reflection makes the fringe dark.

blocks.prompt: Why are interference colours seen on soap bubbles but not on window glass?
blocks.explanation: A soap film is only about a wavelength of light thick, so the two reflections have a small path difference that gives distinct colours. Window glass is millions of wavelengths thick, so the path difference is huge and the colours from slightly different thicknesses and angles overlap and wash out.

items: Thin film: reflections from the top and bottom surfaces interfere; colours depend on thickness.
Air wedge: path difference 2t; contact line dark due to a half-cycle phase shift on reflection.
